newsitem.title: UK: Main UK parties say they'll wait and see on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Main UK parties say they'll wait and see on EMU.

text.p: As Britain's ruling Conservatives go into their annual conference, doubts are widespread that Prime Minister John Major and opposition Labour leader Tony Blair can remain non-commital until the next election on whether Britain should join a European single currency.
Given divisions in both main parties, however, climbing off the fence before the polls, due by next May at the latest, would lead to serious upheaval within both parties.
Here is a guide to their most recent pronouncements on European economic and monetary union (EMU), due to start in 1999.

CONSERVATIVES: Major, who negotiated an opt-out for Britain at the Maastricht conference in 1991, is determined not to yield to vocal right-wing "Euro-sceptics" who believe rejecting a single currency would be a big vote-winner.
The ruling party's long-established position is to decide on EMU when it has to, not before.
Under a compromise thrashed out in cabinet in April, any decision to join during the next five-year parliament would be put to a referendum.
Abandoning this studied neutrality before the election would split the cabinet and almost certainly lead to the resignation of its leading pro-European, finance minister Kenneth Clarke.
Moreover, Major said on Sunday, it would rob Britain of a say in crucial talks on how the single currency will work.

"The argument that we should divorce ourselves from these negotiations now has no intellectual coherence whatever... it is not credible, and it isn't going to happen," he told a BBC television interviewer.
"We can negotiate in Britain's interest, for the advantage of Britain, right up to the 59th minute of the last hour, and then say we're not going in because we don't think it's right."
LABOUR: The main opposition party, pro-EMU in principle, is also divided in practice over Europe.

But leader Blair points to a big difference: unlike the Conservatives, he says, there is no large faction in Labour with deep-seated constitutional objections to scrapping the pound on grounds of lost sovereignty.
Labour's policy was summarised in a pre-election policy blueprint its conference overwhelmingly approved last week.

"For Britain, we would need to be convinced that economic conditions would allow it to succeed. We will therefore reserve our options on it. If there is a decision to join, the consent of the British people will be sought either in a general election or through a referendum," the document said.
But differences among Labour politicians on how to interpret the policy were never far from the surface at the conference.

Aides say pro-European finance spokesman Gordon Brown would like Labour's final election manifesto to contain a form of words that provide a mandate for signing up for EMU in 1999, if the terms are right, without holding a divisive referendum.

Foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook, by contrast, signalled his preference that Britain should not rush into EMU by listing benchmarks for membership that go far beyond the Maastricht treaty's criteria on debt, deficits, inflation and bond yields.
"The single market would work better with a single currency. But Britain will only benefit if we can compete on level terms.

"That is why Labour believes that for Britain to join a single currency we need first to achieve convergence of economic performance in the real world of output, of investment and of jobs," Cook said in his conference speech.

Holding the ring is Blair, who sounded a cautious note last week by warning of the pitfalls of EMU if there was insufficient labour mobility or fiscal transfers to make up for the loss of economic adjustment afforded by exchange rate changes.
But he added: "It is important to recognise that to rule out a single currency for ever would be a serious mistake."
LIBERAL DEMOCRATS - Britain's third party, led by Paddy Ashdown, has no hesitation in saying it would sign up for EMU, subject to the criteria being met and approval in a referendum.

"Every single reason that I know for the benefit of this country points me to the position that if a single currency is formed and Britain can be part of it, Britain should be part of it," Ashdown told his party's conference last month.
He was scathing of Major and Blair for avoiding the issue.
"Britain will be asked to vote without knowing what it is voting for. That is a conspiracy perpetrated on the British people by their politicians," the Lib Dem leader said.
